items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Your liver and your eyes have separate clocks
items.claim: Every cell in your body has its own molecular clock. The 'master' clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) synchronises them. Eating at the wrong time can desynchronise organs from each other — same as jet lag without the travel.
items.prompt: What is a cellular circadian clock made of?

options.text: A transcription-translation feedback loop: genes (BMAL1/CLOCK in mammals) drive expression of inhibitor proteins (PER, CRY) that themselves repress the original genes — the cycle takes about 24 hours to complete
An internal sundial of pigment molecules

items.reveal:
In Drosophila, Hall, Rosbash and Young identified Period (PER) gene and worked out the negative feedback loop: PER protein accumulates in the cell, eventually shuts down its own transcription, then degrades, allowing the cycle to repeat. Mammals have BMAL1/CLOCK driving PER1/2/3 and CRY1/2, with the same logic.

The cycle's intrinsic period is close to 24 hours; light input (via melanopsin in retinal ganglion cells) synchronises it to the day.

Peripheral clocks (in liver, muscle, fat) entrain primarily to feeding times. Eating at midnight tells your liver it's daytime even as your SCN says it's night — exactly the desynchronisation seen in shift workers, who have elevated rates of metabolic disease and some cancers.
items.why: The biological clock is pictured as one master organ. Every cell has one, and keeping them aligned is a daily ongoing process — and easily disrupted.

items.title: Famine in 1944 affected the grandchildren of survivors
items.claim: The Dutch Hongerwinter (1944-1945) caused severe famine for several months. Decades later, the GRANDchildren of women pregnant during the famine showed altered methylation patterns and different rates of metabolic disease — even though they were never themselves underfed.
items.prompt: How does an environmental stress affect three generations?

options.text: Epigenetic marks (especially DNA methylation patterns) acquired during fetal development can persist into adulthood; some can affect germline cells, allowing the next generation to inherit the modified pattern
It must be a DNA sequence mutation caused by famine
Famine alters social behaviour passed to grandchildren culturally

items.reveal_title: Heijmans, Tobi and colleagues — the Hongerwinter epigenetic study
items.reveal:
Heijmans et al. (2008) compared DNA methylation in adults who had been in utero during the Dutch famine to their unexposed siblings. The famine-exposed showed less methylation at the IGF2 gene 60 years later.

More recent work has shown some methylation marks pass to grandchildren, with associated health correlates.

This is not classical Lamarckism (inheritance of acquired characteristics through soft inheritance). Methylation marks are mostly cleared between generations, but some escape erasure. The mechanisms are still being mapped.

Distinguishing real intergenerational inheritance from confounders (in utero exposure, shared environment) requires careful study design. Animal models (rodents) have been used to confirm causal mechanisms.
items.why: Inheritance is taught as DNA sequence transmission. Some heritable information is encoded above the sequence, in modifications to DNA and chromatin — and famine can leave its mark across decades.
